stories.headline: AI sell-off hits Asia hard, but Sensex and rupee rise
stories.question: Why did Asian and US markets crash on AI fears while India rose?
stories.dek: On 20 November, stock markets in Taiwan, Korea and Japan fell more than 5% as AI doubts spread. India rose because bank stocks gained and foreign money flowed in.

so_far.text: Through November 2026, doubts grew about the huge sums spent on artificial intelligence (AI). In remarks reported on 17 November, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said slightly over $1 trillion of AI money moves in circles between firms, and about two-thirds of it is debt. On 19 November she said the AI market correction had "a little bit more" to go. Traders also began betting on a US interest rate rise in December.

what_happened.text: On 19 November, short seller Hunterbrook questioned chipmaker AMD's China business and its exposure to export controls. AMD fell 7.72% to $489.19. Anthropic's market debut that day failed to steady tech shares. The Nasdaq fell 2.3% and the S&P 500 fell 2.0%. On 20 November, Asia followed. Taiwan's Taiex fell 6.2%, ending its worst week since 1991. South Korea's Kospi fell 5.2% and Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 5.1%. Yet India's Sensex rose 1.08% to 83,919.71. The rupee strengthened past 93 per dollar for the first time since April.

steps.text: More and more AI building was paid for with debt: bonds, plus about $3 trillion of commitments kept off company books.
Much AI money moves in circles between firms, so one firm's trouble spreads to its suppliers and customers.
On 19 November, Hunterbrook's short report sent AMD down 7.72%, a shock to chips; Anthropic's debut that day failed to calm tech shares.
Traders expect a US rate rise, which makes borrowed AI money costlier; Georgieva warned AI demand will push rates up worldwide.
Asia's chip-heavy markets fell hardest, while India rose on bank stocks and foreign inflows.

history.text:
This sell-off began with a spending race. In January 2025, DeepSeek built AI models that matched costly ones at a low cost. Nvidia, which makes the chips AI runs on, lost 17% in a day, about $600 billion. It showed how fast hopes about AI could reverse. Yet the race went on: Oracle, OpenAI and SoftBank planned the $500 billion Stargate project.

In July 2025, Nvidia became the first company worth $4 trillion. In September 2025, it announced a $100 billion investment in OpenAI, which buys its chips. Critics call such deals circular: a supplier funds a customer, who then spends the money buying from that supplier. In October 2025, Nvidia passed $5 trillion.

The way the race was paid for changed too. At first, firms paid for AI from their own cash. By 2026, borrowing through bond markets was the main source. On top of that came about $3 trillion of commitments kept off company balance sheets. Debt speeds up a boom and makes a bust sharper. In June and July 2026, South Korea's chip-heavy Kospi fell 44% in 40 days. In November 2026, the doubts returned.

lesson.concept: How a stock index's mix decides its move
lesson.big_idea: A stock index is a weighted average of its companies. If one sector is a big share of it and that sector crashes, the whole index falls hard. An index with a different mix can rise on the same day.

steps.title: An index is a basket
steps.text: A stock index, like the Sensex or Taiwan's Taiex, tracks a basket of big companies. Its daily move is the combined move of everything in the basket.

steps.title: Bigger companies count more
steps.text: Each company has a weight, roughly its share of the basket's total market value. A company that makes up 30% of the basket moves the index three times as much as one at 10%.

steps.title: Weight times move, added up
steps.text: To find a sector's effect, multiply its weight by its own move. Add up every sector's effect, and you get the index's move for the day.

steps.title: Same news, different baskets
steps.text: AI fears hit chip stocks, so chip-heavy markets in Asia fall hardest. On 20 November, TSMC fell 4.8% and SoftBank 14.5%. A market lifted by bank stocks can even rise.

example.setup: Imagine two made-up indexes. Chip Index is 50% chip stocks and 50% other stocks. Bank Index is 40% banks and 60% other stocks. On AI news, chips fall 10%, banks rise 2%, and other stocks stay flat.

lines.label: Chip Index: chips
lines.note: Half the basket loses a tenth of its value.

lines.label: Chip Index: others
lines.note: Flat stocks add nothing.

lines.label: Chip Index total
lines.note: The chip slump drags the whole index down.

lines.label: Bank Index: banks
lines.note: Banks gain as fresh money arrives.

lines.label: Bank Index: others
lines.note: Again, flat stocks add nothing.

lines.label: Bank Index total
lines.note: It rises on the very same day.

example.result: The same day's news pushed one index down 5% and the other up 0.8%. The news did not decide the gap. What each basket held did.

apply.text: That is what happened on 20 November. Asia's chip-heavy markets took the AI hit: TSMC fell 4.8%, and the Taiex, Kospi and Nikkei each fell more than 5%. Bank stocks and foreign inflows lifted the Sensex, so it rose 1.08%. Foreign money also pushed the rupee past 93 per dollar.

practice.q: Say an index is 30% chip stocks and 70% banks. Chips fall 10% and banks rise 1%. What does the index do?
practice.answer: Chips: 30% × −10% = −3%. Banks: 70% × +1% = +0.7%. Add them: −3% + 0.7% = −2.3%. The index falls 2.3%, because the chip loss outweighs the bank gain.

stories.headline: Houthi missile hits Saudi wealth fund's tower in Riyadh
stories.question: Is the Iran war now reaching the Gulf's money centres, not just its oil?
stories.dek: Increasingly, yes. A Houthi missile damaged Saudi Arabia's wealth fund tower on 19 November. It was the second hit on Riyadh's financial district in under two weeks, threatening Saudi plans beyond oil.

so_far.text: The Houthis have also seized territory from Yemen's Saudi-backed government. On 8 November a Houthi strike hit an Aramco building in Riyadh's financial district. It was the first of two landmark hits there in under two weeks. On 18 November Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met Adm. Brad Cooper, chief of US Central Command (CENTCOM). Brent crude, the world's benchmark oil price, was about $95.34 a barrel around 18 November. Before the war it was roughly $72.

what_happened.text: On 19 November 2026 a Houthi missile hit the PIF Tower in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD). It is the city's tallest building and the headquarters of PIF, Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund. Windows were blown out across seven to eight floors, and nearby buildings were damaged. No injuries were reported, and KAFD was closed to visitors. Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry reserved the right to take "all necessary measures". The Houthi-run Saba agency said Saudi aircraft struck Sanaa early that day. On 20 November Iran's navy said a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine east of the Strait of Hormuz. That cause is unconfirmed.

steps.text: The Houthis are Iran's allies, and since the war on Iran began, their fight with Saudi Arabia has flared again.
In July they declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, threatening its Red Sea oil exports through Yanbu.
In November their missiles reached Riyadh's financial district, hitting Aramco and wealth-fund buildings, which are symbols of Saudi money.
Even with no injuries, such strikes can make Riyadh look riskier to investors, visitors and airlines.
Higher risk threatens Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's plans to diversify the Saudi economy beyond oil.

history.text:
The story has two roots. The first is Iran. In 1979 a revolution ended the Shah's rule and cut Iran's ties with the US. In 2018 the US abandoned the 2015 nuclear deal. A Twelve-Day War in June 2025 ended in a ceasefire.

The second root is Yemen. The Houthis took the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014. On 26 March 2015 a Saudi-led coalition intervened to back the Hadi government. That made Saudi Arabia and the Houthis direct enemies. A UN truce began on 2 April 2022 but expired that October.

The two roots joined in 2026. The US and Israel struck Iran on 28 February, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran then blocked the Strait of Hormuz, causing the largest oil supply disruption on record. A ceasefire from 8 April collapsed on 8 July after Iran attacked ships. Around 13 July Saudi strikes hit Sanaa airport, and the Houthis hit Abha airport. On 20 July the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia. That threatened the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which handled about 92% of Saudi seaborne crude exports in June. In November, Houthi missiles began reaching Riyadh's financial district.

lesson.concept: How war risk scares investment away
lesson.big_idea: Investors put money in only when a project's expected return beats the minimum they demand. War raises that minimum, so projects stall even when nothing is destroyed.

steps.title: Investors compare two numbers
steps.text: An investor first estimates a project's yearly return. Then they compare it with the minimum return they demand. If the return is higher than the minimum, they invest. If it is lower, they wait.

steps.title: The minimum has two parts
steps.text: The minimum is a safe return, which is what money earns with almost no danger, plus a risk premium. The risk premium is the extra return demanded for taking on danger.

steps.title: War raises the risk premium
steps.text: Missile strikes, closed districts and cancelled flights make losses more likely. So investors tend to demand a bigger risk premium, even though the project itself has not changed.

steps.title: Some projects stop passing
steps.text: With a higher minimum, projects that once cleared the bar now fall below it. The money is delayed or goes to safer places.

steps.title: Why Saudi Arabia cares
steps.text: Saudi Arabia wants to diversify, meaning to build industries beyond oil. The conflict threatens those plans, and the strikes hit Aramco and the wealth fund's tower.

example.setup: Imagine a company deciding whether to build a ₹100 crore office in a city. It expects ₹10 crore profit a year. Assume money earns 5% a year with almost no danger.

example.result: Nothing about the office changed; only the danger did. A bigger risk premium turned a yes into a wait. That is how strikes that injure no one can still slow an economy.

apply.text: PIF, Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, has its headquarters in Riyadh's financial district. Houthi missiles hit an Aramco building there on 8 November and the PIF Tower on 19 November, and the district closed to visitors. Each strike can raise the risk premium investors attach to Riyadh. That helps explain why the conflict threatens the Crown Prince's plans to diversify the economy.

practice.q: Same ₹100 crore office, but it expects ₹13 crore a year. Does it go ahead after the strikes? What if the premium rises to 10%?
practice.answer: Expected return: ₹13 crore ÷ ₹100 crore = 13%. After the strikes the minimum is 5% + 7% = 12%. 13% beats 12%, so it goes ahead. If the premium rises to 10%, the minimum is 5% + 10% = 15%. 13% is below 15%, so it waits.

stories.headline: Russia rejects NATO-style guarantees, strikes Kyiv; missile crashes in Poland
stories.question: After Shenzhen, are Russia and Ukraine moving towards peace or towards a wider war?
stories.dek: Mostly towards escalation. On 20 November, a day after a US envoy said Russia was 'comfortable' with NATO-style guarantees, Moscow pushed back. It also struck Kyiv's bridges, and a Russian missile crashed in Poland.

so_far.text: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, and the war continues. The United States is trying to broker a deal. On 19 November, the US, Russian and Chinese leaders, Trump, Putin and Xi, met in Shenzhen. They issued a declaration on nuclear risk, with no arms-reduction measures and no Ukraine terms. The same day, at talks in Berlin, US envoy Jared Kushner said Russia was 'comfortable' with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine. Days earlier, on 16–17 November, drones had collapsed a road arch of the Crimean Bridge.

what_happened.text: On 20 November, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov rejected US-floated NATO-style guarantees. He said a 'quasi-membership' arrangement for Ukraine would cross a Russian red line. Overnight into 20 November, Russia fired more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles, 27 of them ballistic, Zelensky said. Strikes hit three Dnipro bridges in Kyiv; reported deaths ranged from six to seven. That morning, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed near Nowy Lipowiec, in Poland's Lublin region. Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called it 'another provocation by Russia'.

steps.text: The Crimean Bridge, Russia's direct link to Crimea, was attacked from the air three times in one week.
Putin called the bridge civilian, warned of a 'painful' response and ruled out negotiations on a partial ceasefire.
Hours later Russia launched one of the war's largest attacks, hitting three bridges over the Dnipro in Kyiv.
On 20 November a Russian Kh-101 crashed in Poland; Poland's defence minister suggested the timing, during nearby Coalition of the Willing exercises, was deliberate.
Russia's narrow terms on guarantees mean the talks Kushner described have no agreed starting point yet.

history.text: The Crimean Bridge story starts in 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine. Russia then built a bridge across the Kerch Strait to link Crimea directly to Russia. The road bridge opened in May 2018 and the rail bridge in December 2019. After Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, the bridge became a target. On 8 October 2022 an explosion damaged its road section and set rail tankers alight. Russia blamed Ukraine. Road traffic reopened only in February 2023. On 17 July 2023, explosions attributed to naval drones collapsed a road section and killed two people. Repairs finished in October 2023. On 3 June 2025, Ukraine's security service, the SBU, set off underwater explosives near the bridge's pillars. Each attack showed the link could be cut, and each repair took months. In October 2026 the fight over bridges widened. Russia struck Kyiv's bridges over the Dnipro river for the first time since the 2022 invasion. Then, on 16–17 November 2026, drones collapsed the arch holding up the Crimean Bridge's road span. A second thread runs through Poland. On 30 July 2026 a Russian Kh-101 missile crashed in Tarnawa-Kolonia, eastern Poland, and Polish and NATO jets scrambled. On guarantees, Putin said in August 2026 that 'every country should have them, Ukraine included'. But Russia has long rejected NATO troops in Ukraine.

lesson.concept: How a security guarantee like NATO's Article 5 works
lesson.big_idea: A security guarantee is a promise that other countries will help defend you if attacked. It works by making an attack too costly, and only if the attacker believes the promise.

steps.title: Start with the fear
steps.text: A country beside a bigger, hostile neighbour fears a fresh attack. A ceasefire alone does not remove that fear, because nothing stops the neighbour trying again later.

steps.title: A promise from outside
steps.text: A security guarantee is other countries promising to help if that attack comes. It aims to make attacking too costly to try. This is called deterrence.

steps.title: Article 5 is the strongest form
steps.text: In NATO, Article 5 treats an attack on one member as an attack on all. Each member then takes the action it judges necessary, which can include armed force.

steps.title: 'Article 5-style' copies the promise
steps.text: Ukraine is not in NATO. An 'Article 5-style' guarantee would give it a similar promise without membership. Kushner said on 19 November that Russia was comfortable with this.

steps.title: Why Russia draws a red line
steps.text: If the promise is as strong as NATO's, the label hardly matters. Ryabkov called it 'quasi-membership', a red line; reportedly Moscow wants Kyiv to renounce NATO first.

example.setup: Imagine Bigland is weighing an attack on its small neighbour, Smallland. Say Bigland scores the gain at 10 points, and the cost of fighting Smallland alone at 6 points.

lines.label: No guarantee
lines.note: Positive, so attacking looks worth it.

lines.label: Three allies join
lines.note: The promise raises the price of attacking.

lines.label: New total cost
lines.note: Fighting Smallland and its backers together.

lines.label: With the guarantee
lines.note: Negative, so attacking now looks like a losing move.

lines.label: Only half believed
lines.note: Barely deterred: a doubtful promise only just works.

example.result: A guarantee stops an attack by raising its cost, and only if the attacker believes the allies will act. A strong, believable promise flips +4 into −5.

apply.text: This explains the clash. On 19 November Kushner said Russia was comfortable with Article 5-style guarantees. But a strong, believable promise is exactly what turns Bigland's +4 into −5. So on 20 November Ryabkov called it 'quasi-membership' and a red line, and Moscow reportedly wants Kyiv to renounce NATO first.

practice.q: Same Bigland, but only two allies sign, each adding a cost of 3. Does attacking still look worth it?
practice.answer: Allies add 2 × 3 = 6. Total cost: 6 + 6 = 12. Net: 10 − 12 = −2. Still negative, so attacking looks like a losing move, but the margin is smaller than with three allies (−5).

scenes.say: Ab is sab ke peeche ka ek idea: security guarantee kaam kaise karti hai. Dushman padosi ke bagal wala desh naye hamle se darta hai, ceasefire ke baad bhi. Guarantee matlab doosre desh vaada karte hain ki uski hifazat mein madad karenge. Yeh hamle ko bahut mehenga bana kar kaam karti hai. Ise kehte hain deterrence.
scenes.speak: अब इस सब के पीछे का एक idea: security guarantee काम कैसे करती है। दुश्मन पड़ोसी के बग़ल वाला देश नए हमले से डरता है, ceasefire के बाद भी। Guarantee मतलब दूसरे देश वादा करते हैं कि उसकी हिफ़ाज़त में मदद करेंगे। यह हमले को बहुत महँगा बना कर काम करती है। इसे कहते हैं deterrence।

scenes.say: Sabse mazboot version hai NATO ka Article 5: ek member par hamla, sab par hamla. Har member khud tay karta hai ki jawab kaise dena hai, aur usmein force bhi shaamil ho sakta hai. 'Article 5 jaisi' guarantee Ukraine ko NATO join kiye bina waisa hi vaada deti hai. Russia kehta hai ki yeh naam ke alawa poori membership hi hai.
scenes.show: Article 5: attack on one, attack on all
scenes.speak: सबसे मज़बूत version है NATO का Article 5: एक member पर हमला, सब पर हमला। हर member ख़ुद तय करता है कि जवाब कैसे देना है, और उसमें force भी शामिल हो सकता है। 'Article 5 जैसी' guarantee Ukraine को NATO join किए बिना वैसा ही वादा देती है। Russia कहता है कि यह नाम के अलावा पूरी membership ही है।

scenes.say: Chaliye ek example dekhte hain. Maan lijiye Bigland, Smallland par hamle ki soch raha hai. Woh fayda 10 points ka aankta hai. Akele Smallland se ladne ki keemat 6 points. 10 minus 6, plus 4. Hamla faydemand lagta hai. Ab 3 allies har ek 3 ki keemat jodte hain. Matlab 9 aur.
scenes.show: Without allies, attack looks worth it
scenes.speak: चलिए एक example देखते हैं। मान लीजिए Bigland, Smallland पर हमले की सोच रहा है। वो फ़ायदा 10 points का आँकता है। अकेले Smallland से लड़ने की क़ीमत 6 points। 10 minus 6, plus 4। हमला फ़ायदेमंद लगता है। अब 3 allies हर एक 3 की क़ीमत जोड़ते हैं। मतलब 9 और।

scenes.say: Total cost: 6 plus 9, barabar 15. 10 minus 15, minus 5. Ab hamla ghaate ka sauda lagta hai. Lekin agar Bigland aadhe vaade par hi bharosa kare, toh cost saadhe das hogi, aur result minus aadha point. Bas kisi tarah roka gaya. Guarantee tabhi kaam karti hai jab us par bharosa ho.
scenes.show: A guarantee works only if believed
scenes.speak: Total cost: 6 plus 9, बराबर 15। 10 minus 15, minus 5। अब हमला घाटे का सौदा लगता है। लेकिन अगर Bigland आधे वादे पर ही भरोसा करे, तो cost साढ़े दस होगी, और result minus आधा point। बस किसी तरह रोका गया। Guarantee तभी काम करती है जब उस पर भरोसा हो।

scenes.say: Toh kaun kya keh raha hai? Ryabkov quasi NATO membership ko red line kehte hain, aur reports ke mutabik chahte hain ki Kyiv pehle NATO ka iraada chhode. Kushner kehte hain Russia guarantees se comfortable hai. Putin painful jawab ka vaada karte hain. Poland ke minister ko timing jaan boojhkar lagti hai, kyunki paas mein Coalition of the Willing ki exercises chal rahi hain.
scenes.speak: तो कौन क्या कह रहा है? Ryabkov quasi NATO membership को red line कहते हैं, और reports के मुताबिक़ चाहते हैं कि Kyiv पहले NATO का इरादा छोड़े। Kushner कहते हैं Russia guarantees से comfortable है। Putin painful जवाब का वादा करते हैं। Poland के minister को timing जान बूझकर लगती है, क्योंकि पास में Coalition of the Willing की exercises चल रही हैं।

scenes.say: Ek aam myth: NATO desh mein Russian missile gire toh seedha jung. Aisa nahi hai. Article 5 ke tahat har member khud tay karta hai ki jawab kaise de. July 2026 mein jab Poland mein Kh 101 giri thi, tab jets scramble hue aur violation ki ninda hui. Nayi crash par NATO level ka koi jawab ab tak nahi mila hai.
scenes.show: Myth: missile in NATO means automatic war
scenes.speak: एक आम myth: NATO देश में Russian missile गिरे तो सीधा जंग। ऐसा नहीं है। Article 5 के तहत हर member ख़ुद तय करता है कि जवाब कैसे दे। July 2026 में जब Poland में Kh 101 गिरी थी, तब jets scramble हुए और violation की निंदा हुई। नई crash पर NATO level का कोई जवाब अब तक नहीं मिला है।

scenes.say: India mein aapke liye iska kya matlab hai? Ab tak prices, jobs ya travel par koi seedha asar nahi hai. Lekin isse dikhta hai ki Ukraine ki security par, jo kisi bhi deal ka core hai, Russia aur West ab bhi kitne door hain. Aur NATO desh mein missile girna jung ko phaila sakta hai.
scenes.speak: India में आपके लिए इसका क्या मतलब है? अब तक prices, jobs या travel पर कोई सीधा असर नहीं है। लेकिन इससे दिखता है कि Ukraine की security पर, जो किसी भी deal का core है, Russia और West अब भी कितने दूर हैं। और NATO देश में missile गिरना जंग को फैला सकता है।

scenes.say: Wapas apne lesson par. Kushner ne ek mazboot, Article 5 jaisa vaada saamne rakha. Hamare example mein mazboot vaada plus 4 ko minus 5 bana deta hai. Russia ko theek isi baat ka darr hai, isliye Ryabkov ne ise red line kaha.
scenes.speak: वापस अपने lesson पर। Kushner ने एक मज़बूत, Article 5 जैसा वादा सामने रखा। हमारे example में मज़बूत वादा plus 4 को minus 5 बना देता है। Russia को ठीक इसी बात का डर है, इसलिए Ryabkov ने इसे red line कहा।

scenes.say: Aage kya dekhna hai. Kya Russia ki jawabi karwai khatam hui? Kya NATO Poland crash par formally jawab dega? Aur kya talks ki koi date tay hogi? Putin kehte hain ab tak koi date tay nahi hui, aur Kremlin ne European officials ko Moscow bulaya hai. Kyiv ka final toll bhi saaf nahi hai.
scenes.show: No date yet for next talks
scenes.speak: आगे क्या देखना है। क्या Russia की जवाबी कार्रवाई ख़त्म हुई? क्या NATO Poland crash पर formally जवाब देगा? और क्या talks की कोई date तय होगी? Putin कहते हैं अब तक कोई date तय नहीं हुई, और Kremlin ने European officials को Moscow बुलाया है। Kyiv का final toll भी साफ़ नहीं है।

scenes.say: Teen baatein yaad rakhiye. Security guarantee hamle ki keemat badha kar use rokti hai, lekin tabhi jab us par bharosa ho. 20 November ko Russia ne NATO jaisi guarantees thukrayi aur Kyiv par zor se hamla kiya, jo jaldi peace se door ishara karta hai. Aage dekhiye: aur jawabi karwai, NATO ka response, aur talks ki date.

scenes.speak: तीन बातें याद रखिए। Security guarantee हमले की क़ीमत बढ़ा कर उसे रोकती है, लेकिन तभी जब उस पर भरोसा हो। 20 November को Russia ने NATO जैसी guarantees ठुकराईं और Kyiv पर ज़ोर से हमला किया, जो जल्दी peace से दूर इशारा करता है। आगे देखिए: और जवाबी कार्रवाई, NATO का response, और talks की date।

stories.headline: Japan's forces will fire missiles on Indian ranges for the first time
stories.question: Why would Japan fire its missiles on Indian ranges instead of at home?
stories.dek: Japan does not have enough room at home for long-distance live firing. On 19 November 2026 India agreed to host Japanese missile training. It is a big step in fast-growing India–Japan defence ties.

so_far.text: Japan's armed forces are called the Self-Defence Forces. In 2026 Japan put a new, longer-range missile into service. It also loosened its rules on selling weapons abroad. India's Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and Japan's Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi met three times in 2026: in August, October and November. In August, Japan said it wanted to explore using Indian firing ranges. In mid-October, Japanese officials spent about a week inspecting Indian test facilities.

what_happened.text: On 19 November 2026 in Tokyo, India and Japan signed a letter of intent, a formal statement of what both plan to do. It allows Japan's Self-Defence Forces to hold live-fire training at Indian ranges for the first time. This includes surface-to-ship missile exercises. Business Standard reported the tests will start in 2027. The signing came during Rajnath Singh's 18–19 November visit. The two sides also agreed on a working group for joint naval shipbuilding. DRDO and Japan's ATLA will cooperate on missile technology. Japan has offered to build its Mogami-class warship design in India.

steps.text: Japan now has longer-range missiles; the Type-25, in service since March 2026, is widely believed to reach about 1,000 km.
Firing that far needs closed airspace, safety zones at sea and cleared ranges, which are hard to arrange inside Japan.
On 20 August 2026 Koizumi said Japan wanted to explore using ranges in India.
In mid-October 2026 Japanese officials spent about a week inspecting Indian test facilities and ranges.
So on 19 November 2026 they signed a letter allowing Japanese live-fire missile training in India.

history.text:
The story starts with a new missile. In March 2026 Japan's Type-25 stand-off missile entered service in Kumamoto. A stand-off missile is one fired from far away, beyond an enemy's reach. The Type-25 is widely believed to fly about 1,000 km, five times as far as the older Type 12. But Japan lacks suitable places at home to practise such long shots.

On 21 April 2026 Japan's cabinet loosened its export rules. It lifted limits on selling finished lethal equipment to 17 partner countries. This was a wider change in Japan's defence policy. The reports do not say whether India is one of the 17.

On 20 August 2026 Koizumi said Japan wanted to explore using ranges in India. The same day, the two countries signed a maritime security arrangement in New Delhi. Both sides also wanted an early deal to co-develop and co-produce UNICORN, a mast-shaped antenna used on Japanese warships. It was described as their first defence equipment transfer project.

In mid-October 2026 Japanese officials spent about a week inspecting Indian ranges. The talks were bilateral, meaning between the two countries only, and not linked to the Quad grouping. On 19 November the letter of intent turned the idea into a plan.

analogy.text: Think of a cricket academy in a crowded city. Its nets are too small for batters to practise full-power shots. So it books a large ground in a friendly town. Japan is doing the same: borrowing India's open ranges for long-distance firing.
analogy.breaks: A missile range must also empty the sky and sea of planes and ships. Hosting a foreign military is a political choice, not a rental.

lesson.concept: Why long-range missile tests need so much space
lesson.big_idea: A missile test needs an empty stretch of sky and sea along its whole flight path. The farther the missile flies, the bigger that area, and the harder it is to find.

steps.title: Every test needs a danger zone
steps.text: Before a live firing, the military marks a danger zone: the airspace and sea the missile and its debris might cross. Planes are sent around it, and ships are told to stay out until the firing ends.

steps.title: The zone follows the flight path
steps.text: A simple way to picture the zone is a long strip. The missile's range is its length. A safety margin on each side is its width. Length times width gives the area to clear.

steps.title: Longer range, much bigger strip
steps.text: Japan's Type 12 missile is believed to fly about 200 km. The newer Type-25 is believed to fly about 1,000 km. Keep the width the same, and the strip becomes five times longer, so five times the area.

steps.title: Japan finds this hard at home
steps.text: Firing that far needs airspace management, maritime safety zones and range clearance. These are hard to arrange inside Japan. So Japan looked to India, whose ranges its officials inspected for about a week in October 2026.

example.result: Five times the range means five times the sky and sea to empty. A country short of open space at home may find it easier to borrow a partner's range.

apply.text: This is the gap India fills. Long-distance live firing needs airspace and sea zones that are hard to arrange in Japan. The 19 November letter lets Japan's forces fire surface-to-ship missiles on Indian ranges, reportedly from 2027. Japan has not said whether the Type-25 will be one of them.

practice.q: Suppose a missile flies 500 km and the safety strip is 30 km wide. How big is the area, and how does it compare with a 200 km shot of the same width?
practice.answer: Area: 500 × 30 = 15,000 sq km. The 200 km shot: 200 × 30 = 6,000 sq km. 15,000 ÷ 6,000 = 2.5. So the longer shot needs two and a half times the space.

stories.headline: Pakistani minister in Delhi, Nepal's PM next: a thaw, or not?
stories.question: Does a Pakistani minister in Delhi and Nepal's PM visiting mean India's neighbourhood is thawing?
stories.dek: Not with Pakistan. Malik came for a forum of many SCO countries, and India says its policy is unchanged. Nepal is different. Its new PM comes for one-to-one talks on aid, flights and borders.

so_far.text: India and Pakistan have barely engaged since tourists were attacked at Pahalgam on 22 April 2025. In May 2025 India hit back with the Operation Sindoor strikes. It also put the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, meaning paused. Pakistan suspended the Shimla Agreement, closed its airspace and halted trade. In Nepal, youth-led protests brought down the government in 2025. In March 2026, Balendra Shah beat KP Sharma Oli by 49,614 votes, and his party won about two-thirds of the 275 seats. In May 2026, The Wire reported that Nepal protested India's use of the Lipulekh route for the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra.

what_happened.text: On 20 November, reports said Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik had arrived in New Delhi. He leads Pakistan's delegation to the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, a three-day event. DW reports it is the first visit to India by a Pakistani federal minister since 2023. No India–Pakistan meeting has been announced. India's foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India invited all SCO members. He said its Pakistan policy 'remains in place; there has been no change'. Separately, Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah visits India from 22 November. Talks with Modi are expected on 23 November.

steps.text: A host of an SCO event invites every member country, and India says it invited all of them.
Attending a group event is not the same as holding talks, and no India–Pakistan meeting has been announced.
India says its post-Pahalgam policy is unchanged. So the paused water treaty and the missing high commissioners both remain.
Nepal's visit is bilateral, meaning one-to-one. Its PM comes for India alone, with aid, flights and projects to discuss.
Signed deals with Nepal would show real movement, but the Kalapani, Limpiyadhura and Susta border disputes remain unresolved.

history.text:
Two old stories meet here. Nepal's begins in 1816. That year the Treaty of Sugauli made the Kali River Nepal's western boundary. Later British maps placed the river's source in a different spot, and that gap grew into the Kalapani dispute. In 1950 a Treaty of Peace and Friendship set the rules for India–Nepal security, trade and transit. Nepal wants the treaty reviewed. India agreed in 2014 to revise it, but how is still unclear.

Pakistan's story begins with Partition in 1947. It displaced up to 15 million people and started the Kashmir dispute. Wars followed in 1947–48, 1965 and 1971. Then the 1972 Shimla Agreement committed both sides to settle disputes bilaterally, meaning between the two of them only.

After that, trust broke down step by step. The 2008 Mumbai attacks killed 175 people and stopped the dialogue. The 2016 Uri attack and the February 2019 Pulwama attack raised tensions further. In August 2019 India revoked Kashmir's special status. Neither country has had a high commissioner in the other's capital since 2019.

Nepal's ties frayed too. In 2015 Madhesi protests blockaded the border. Nepal blamed India for the blocked supplies, and India denied it. In 2020 the two argued over India's road to Lipulekh. Then the April 2025 Pahalgam attack left India–Pakistan ties largely frozen. In March 2026 Nepal elected a new leader, Balendra Shah.

lesson.concept: How bilateral and multilateral diplomacy differ
lesson.big_idea: Bilateral diplomacy is two countries dealing directly. Multilateral diplomacy happens in a group of many. Rivals can sit in the same group meeting without making up, so a real thaw shows up in one-to-one steps.

steps.title: Bilateral means two countries
steps.text: Bilateral diplomacy is when two countries deal only with each other. That means visits, leader-to-leader talks and signed agreements. In the 1972 Shimla Agreement, India and Pakistan promised to settle disputes this way.

steps.title: Multilateral means a group
steps.text: Multilateral diplomacy happens in a club of many countries, like the SCO. When a member hosts an event, it normally invites every member, friend or rival. India said it invited all SCO members.

steps.title: Same room, not same table
steps.text: At a group event, rivals can share a hall and never talk alone. Optional side talks are called meetings 'on the sidelines'. No India–Pakistan sideline meeting has been announced.

steps.title: What a real thaw looks like
steps.text: A thaw shows up as bilateral steps: sending back high commissioners, reviving a paused treaty, reopening trade. With Pakistan, none of these has happened. India still keeps the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance.

example.setup: Imagine a book club of eight families that meets at a different home each month. Two of them, the Sharmas and the Mehtas, fell out years ago and stopped visiting each other.

lines.label: Stage 1: the invite
lines.calc: Sharmas host; all eight families are invited
lines.note: Club rule: the host invites every member, friend or not.

lines.label: Stage 2: attending
lines.calc: Mehtas come for the book discussion
lines.note: They come for the club, not for the hosts.

lines.label: Stage 3: the side chat
lines.calc: Sharmas and Mehtas talk alone? Nothing planned
lines.note: This is the 'sidelines' test.

lines.label: Stage 4: the real signal
lines.calc: A private dinner between the two? Not yet
lines.note: That would be a bilateral step.

lines.label: Compare: the Guptas
lines.calc: Guptas visit the Sharmas alone, with an agenda
lines.note: A one-to-one visit is bilateral by design.

example.result: Sitting in the same room at a group event shows only that both families still follow the club's rules. Making up needs a one-to-one step, like the Guptas' visit.

apply.text: Malik's trip is Stage 2. Pakistan is attending an SCO forum India hosts, but no bilateral meeting is announced and India says its policy is unchanged. Shah's visit is like the Guptas'. It is his first bilateral trip, with talks on 23 November on flood aid, air routes and projects.

practice.q: Suppose India hosts an SCO meeting, and India's and Pakistan's foreign ministers hold a separate one-hour meeting there. Is that meeting bilateral or multilateral?
practice.answer: Step 1: the main event is multilateral, because many members attend. Step 2: the separate meeting involves only two countries. Step 3: so it is bilateral, even though it happened at a multilateral event. It would send a stronger signal than simply attending.

stories.headline: EPFO approves PF payouts in instalments for retiring members
stories.question: EPFO now lets retirees take PF in instalments: how does it work and who should use it?
stories.dek: Retiring members will be able to take their PF as monthly, quarterly or half-yearly payouts while the rest keeps earning. The tax rules and the start date are still pending.

so_far.text: The Employees' Provident Fund (EPF) is a retirement savings account for salaried workers. Money is set aside from each month's salary and builds up over a working life. The Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) runs it. At retirement, members have taken their PF savings as one lump sum. That lump sum is generally tax-free after five years of continuous service. From then on, making the money last was the retiree's own job.

what_happened.text: On 19 November 2026, EPFO's Central Board of Trustees approved a voluntary Systematic Withdrawal Plan at its 240th meeting. Retiring members can take their PF savings in regular instalments instead of one lump sum. They can choose monthly, quarterly or half-yearly payouts. The balance left behind keeps earning returns, and the plan is described as lifelong. If a member dies, nominees or dependants can withdraw the rest or keep the payments going. The board also cut the minimum balance kept in EPF accounts from 25% to 10%. It cut the wait for final settlement from 12 months to two months.

steps.text: A lump sum arrives once, so the retiree alone must make it last for many years.
Under the new plan, the money stays with EPFO and comes out in monthly, quarterly or half-yearly instalments.
Money still inside the account keeps earning returns, so the balance falls more slowly than the payouts add up.
In the first phase, about 6.32 lakh members over 55 with balances above ₹5 lakh are expected to be the main beneficiaries.
Whether instalments beat a lump sum depends on tax and the interest rate, and neither is settled yet.

history.text:
India's provident fund story began about a century ago. A provident fund is a savings pot built from a worker's wages, for old age. A limited Provident Fund Act came in 1925. In 1929 a Royal Commission called for provident funds for industrial workers. The first big scheme followed in 1948: the Coal Mines Provident Fund Scheme.

On 15 November 1951 an ordinance took effect, and EPFO traces its roots to it. The Employees' Provident Funds Act, 1952 replaced the ordinance. The EPF Scheme was fully in force by 1 November 1952.

Over the next decades, protection was added on top of the savings. A Family Pension Scheme came in 1971. The Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme (EDLI), which ties insurance cover to PF deposits, began in 1976. On 19 November 1995 the Employees' Pension Scheme (EPS-95) replaced the 1971 family pension.

In 2014 two changes widened and modernised the system. On 1 September 2014 the wage ceiling, the salary cap used for PF rules, rose from ₹6,500 to ₹15,000 a month. A minimum pension of ₹1,000 was introduced at the same time. On 1 October 2014 the Universal Account Number (UAN) made PF portable, so one account follows a worker from employer to employer.

The new plan changes a different part of the system: how the savings leave the account at retirement. Instead of only one lump sum, members will be able to choose regular instalments.

lesson.concept: How taking savings in instalments stretches them
lesson.big_idea: When you take savings out bit by bit, the money still waiting keeps earning returns. So your pot shrinks more slowly than the total you are paid.

steps.title: Lump sum: everything at once
steps.text: At retirement, PF savings have been paid out as one lump sum. The whole amount leaves the EPF account in one go. After that, you decide how to save, invest or spend it.

steps.title: Instalments: a little at a time
steps.text: Under the Systematic Withdrawal Plan, you choose how often you are paid: monthly, quarterly or half-yearly. Each instalment comes out of your balance, and the rest stays in your account.

steps.title: The rest keeps earning
steps.text: The money still in the account keeps earning returns. So each year, subtract what you took out, then add interest on what is left. EPFO has not said what rate will apply.

steps.title: Tax can change the answer
steps.text: A PF lump sum is generally tax-free after five years of continuous service. Annuity payouts are taxed fully at your slab rate. How instalments will be taxed is still being worked out with the Finance Ministry.

apply.text: This is what EPFO's board approved on 19 November 2026. A retiree like Meena could pick monthly, quarterly or half-yearly payouts while the balance keeps earning. About 6.32 lakh members over 55 with above ₹5 lakh are expected to be the main first-phase beneficiaries. Until the rate and tax rules are set, nobody can do Meena's sum with real numbers.

practice.q: Same ₹10 lakh and the same assumed 8% rate, but Meena takes ₹2 lakh a year. What is left at the end of year 1?
practice.answer: Take out ₹2 lakh: ₹10,00,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹8,00,000. Interest: 8% of ₹8,00,000 = ₹64,000. End of year: ₹8,00,000 + ₹64,000 = ₹8,64,000. Bigger instalments leave less money earning, so the pot shrinks faster.

stories.headline: India launches its first home-made bird flu vaccine for chickens
stories.question: India now has its own bird flu vaccine for chickens: what changes for H5N1 control?
stories.dek: India now has a cheap, home-made vaccine matched to its main bird flu strain. It could cut losses from culling. It works only if enough birds get it, and testing must continue.

so_far.text: H5N1 is a highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), a bird flu that kills poultry fast. India has fought it by finding infected flocks and culling them. Vaccination against HPAI was not allowed. In 2026 an outbreak at Navapur, Maharashtra, led to over 1.5 lakh chickens being culled. As of May, officials reported no human infections in India in 2026. In November 2026, Tamil Nadu reportedly stepped up surveillance around Namakkal, a major egg hub.

what_happened.text: On 20 November 2026, Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan dedicated India's first indigenous H5N1 vaccine for chickens to the nation. ICAR-NIHSAD in Bhopal developed it. It is inactivated, meaning it is made from killed virus. It targets clade 2.3.2.1a, which the government says causes most outbreaks in Indian chickens. Before this, no commercial vaccine made for this clade was available in India. Mint reports a price of ₹1–2 per dose. Officials project that one shot protects a chicken for up to six months. The sources reviewed gave no published trial or efficacy data.

steps.text: India's rule has been to find infected flocks fast and cull them, so the virus runs out of birds.
Culling works, but each outbreak destroys flocks and income; chicken prices fell from ₹110 to below ₹60 a kg in April 2025.
A vaccine matched to clade 2.3.2.1a, behind most Indian chicken outbreaks, can help birds resist infection before it arrives.
At ₹1–2 a dose it is cheap, but it protects a flock only if enough birds get it.
Vaccines may not fully stop infection or spread, so testing, biosecurity and culling stay as the backstop.

history.text:
India's bird flu story begins in Navapur, Maharashtra. Birds there began dying from 24 January 2006. The signs were mistaken for Ranikhet (Newcastle) disease, so officials were not alerted for over two weeks. India confirmed its first H5N1 outbreak on 18 February 2006, and culling began the next day. Losses were estimated at ₹2,200–3,000 crore.

Under India's National Action Plan, the policy has been 'detect and cull': find infected flocks and kill them. Vaccination against HPAI was not allowed. Since 2006, India has recorded more than 500 H5N1 and H5N8 outbreaks. A human H5N1 death was reported in Haryana in 2021.

On 13 October 2023, WOAH accepted India's self-declaration that 26 poultry compartments were free of HPAI. The government says this helps exports. The same year, India allowed vaccination against H9N2, a milder flu, but still not against HPAI. In July 2024 a high-level meeting again chose surveillance and culling. It said mass vaccination with the vaccines then available did not suit India's scattered, backyard-dominated poultry sector.

In April 2025, bird flu reports pushed farm-gate chicken prices below ₹60 a kg. Producers said vaccination should happen only if every bird is covered. A two-year-old in Andhra Pradesh who had eaten raw chicken died of H5N1, believed to be in 2025. In 2026 Navapur was hit again, and over 1.5 lakh chickens were culled.

analogy.text: Culling is like a fire brigade pulling down the houses around a fire, so the fire has nothing left to burn. Vaccination is like fireproofing houses beforehand. Fireproofing only stops a blaze spreading if most houses on the street are treated.
analogy.breaks: A fireproofed house stays safe, but a vaccinated chicken may still catch and pass on the virus. Its protection also fades within months.

for_you.text: If you farm, trade or sell poultry, each outbreak means culled flocks and price crashes. In April 2025, farm-gate chicken fell from ₹110 to below ₹60 a kg. lesson.concept: How vaccinating enough birds stops an outbreak
lesson.big_idea: An outbreak grows when each sick bird infects more than one other. Vaccination protects some of those birds. Once enough are protected, each case causes less than one new case, and the outbreak fades.

steps.title: Each sick bird passes it on
steps.text: Count how many healthy birds one sick bird infects, on average. Call this the spread number. If it is above 1, cases multiply. If it is below 1, the outbreak dies out.

steps.title: A vaccine trains the immune system
steps.text: An inactivated vaccine uses killed virus. The bird's body learns to recognise the virus without getting sick. India's new vaccine is inactivated and matched to clade 2.3.2.1a, the branch behind most Indian chicken outbreaks.

steps.title: Protected birds break the chain
steps.text: When a sick bird meets a vaccinated bird, the virus is far less likely to pass on. So the spread number shrinks in line with the share of birds left unprotected.

steps.title: Enough coverage tips it below 1
steps.text: The tipping point is 1 minus (1 ÷ spread number). Below that coverage, outbreaks keep growing. Above it, each case causes less than one new case.

steps.title: Not perfect, and it fades
steps.text: Vaccines may not fully stop infection or spread, so testing, biosecurity and culling stay as a backstop. Officials project one shot lasts up to six months, so flocks need repeat doses.

In July 2024 the government said mass vaccination did not suit India's backyard-dominated sector. Producers want every bird done. practice.q: Suppose each sick bird infects 5 others. Is vaccinating 70% of the flock enough to make the outbreak shrink?
practice.answer: Unprotected share: 100% − 70% = 30%. New cases per sick bird: 5 × 30% = 1.5. That is above 1, so the outbreak still grows. Tipping point: 1 − 1/5 = 80%. You need more than 80% coverage.

stories.headline: New US chip rule pauses TSMC and Samsung shipments to China
stories.question: Who gets hurt when US rules pause TSMC and Samsung chip shipments to China?
stories.dek: Chinese chip buyers and phone makers wait first, as shipments halt until US licences come through. Malaysian data centres and Nvidia, now under a California subpoena, also face pressure. India is not named.

so_far.text: Since October 2022 the US has limited which advanced chips China can buy. On 16 November 2026 BIS, the Commerce Department agency that runs export controls, issued a rule. It requires licences for advanced AI chips sent to data centres in Singapore, Indonesia, Brazil, Malaysia and Thailand. It also restricts remote access to computing power abroad. Nvidia's longtime CEO Jensen Huang has left after a scandal. A New York Times report says Nvidia chips at YTL's Johor data centre were run for Alibaba by Megaspeed's Speedmatrix unit, bypassing US curbs.

what_happened.text: A BIS rule introduced on 16 November 2026 took effect on 19 November, reports say. Chipmakers using US technology now need export licences to sell certain chips to Chinese customers. The rule removed an exemption that let foundries, factories that make chips for other firms, ship after certifying a chip was not controlled. Even smartphone chips now need case-by-case approval. TSMC and Samsung told Chinese customers they were halting some shipments while they apply, the Financial Times reported via Korean outlets. Samsung's customers include Kunlun and ByteDance. On 19 November California's Attorney General subpoenaed Nvidia; its shares fell 3.3%.

steps.text: Chips made in Taiwan or Korea still rely on US technology, so US export rules can reach them.
Foundries used to certify themselves that a chip was not controlled, then ship without waiting.
The rule removed that exemption, so even smartphone chips now need case-by-case US approval.
Until licences arrive, TSMC and Samsung pause shipments, so Chinese buyers and phone makers wait.
Waiting can delay production even if approval comes, so the impact reaches everyday phones and developers outside China.

history.text: The story starts in October 2022. The US first restricted exports of high-end chips to China and tightened sales of chipmaking equipment, citing national security. In December 2022 it blacklisted 36 Chinese companies, cutting their access to American chipmaking technology. Firms then designed around the limits. In October 2023, after a new Huawei smartphone chip raised alarm, the US widened curbs to Nvidia's weaker China-only A800 and H800 chips. Nvidia answered with an even weaker chip, the H20. In January 2025 China's DeepSeek chatbot topped Apple's US download charts, deepening US worry about Chinese AI. That month, the Biden administration's AI Diffusion rule placed India in a second tier needing licences and chip caps. The Trump administration rescinded it in May 2025. In April 2025 the US required licences for H20 sales to China, and Nvidia expected about $5.5 billion in charges. In July 2025 Washington pledged to lift that, and H20 sales resumed. From December 2025 to May 2026, Commerce approved about 879,000 advanced Nvidia and AMD chips for Chinese firms, out of 3.4 million requested. In November 2026 the new rule removed the exemption that let foundries self-certify chips and ship. Taipei Times, citing sources, says the rules close a manufacturing loophole.

lesson.concept: How a US licence rule can stop chips made abroad
lesson.big_idea: US export rules can reach chips made in Taiwan or Korea if US technology was used. When a quick self-check is replaced by case-by-case licences, shipments stop until approval, and the wait itself does damage.

steps.title: A licence is permission
steps.text: An export licence is government permission to send certain goods abroad. Without it, the seller must not ship. The US began using such limits on advanced chips for China in October 2022.

steps.title: US rules follow US technology
steps.text: A foundry is a factory that makes chips other firms design. Under the new BIS rule, chipmakers using US technology need export licences to sell certain chips to Chinese customers, even when the factory is outside America.

steps.title: The old shortcut: self-certify
steps.text: Until now, foundries and approved packaging and testing firms could check a chip themselves, certify it was not export-controlled, and ship it. There was no wait for Washington.

steps.title: Case-by-case means a queue
steps.text: The rule removed that exemption. Even smartphone chips now need case-by-case US approval. While applications are pending, TSMC and Samsung have paused some shipments to Chinese customers.

steps.title: Delay hurts even if approved
steps.text: Commerce is likely to grant smartphone-chip licences. But a factory waiting for chips cannot build its products. So how long approval takes matters, not only whether it comes.

example.setup: Suppose a phone maker in China buys 1 lakh chips a month from a foundry. It keeps one month of chips in stock. Assume a licence takes three months.

practice.q: Same phone maker, but it keeps two months of stock and the licence takes four months. How many chips is it short?
practice.answer: Chips not shipped: 1 lakh × 4 months = 4 lakh. Stock covers two months: 2 lakh. Shortfall: 4 lakh − 2 lakh = 2 lakh chips, or two months of phones it cannot build.

stories.headline: Shah says Kashmir has no local militants left, but foreign ones remain
stories.question: What is PRAHAAR, and is Kashmir really free of local militants?
stories.dek: Home Minister Amit Shah says Lateef Bhat's killing left Kashmir with no India-born militants. Records do show a sharp fall. But an estimated 40–50 foreign militants remain, and PRAHAAR's own text admits gaps.

so_far.text: On 23 February 2026 the Home Ministry released PRAHAAR, India's first formal national counter-terrorism policy. The name means "strike". Its seven pillars are prevention, swift response, whole-of-government capacity, human rights and rule of law, tackling causes such as radicalisation, international cooperation, and recovery. In November, violence returned to Jammu and Kashmir (J&K). On 11 November militants attacked a CRPF post at Akhran in Kulgam, injuring three. Within 24 hours two Special Police Officers were killed in Kishtwar. On 18 November Lateef Bhat, 22, a Lashkar-e-Taiba militant wanted over the Kulgam attack, was killed in Kulgam.

what_happened.text: On 19 November 2026, Union Home Minister Amit Shah spoke at the National Investigation Agency's two-day counter-terrorism conference in Delhi. He said Kashmir is free of India-born terrorists for the first time in 35 years, after Bhat's killing. Police records had named Bhat the only surviving active local militant in the Valley. Shah also announced a uniform counter-terror strategy for every police station. He blamed past poor coordination between state police and central agencies. He said 16 new NIA branch offices and two zonal offices were approved. He did not define "India-born", and no outside check of the Bhat operation was reported.

steps.text: Security forces count local and foreign militants separately; each count falls when militants are killed, arrested or surrender.
Records show the local count fell from 50–60 five years ago to 17 in May 2025, then one in 2026.
Police records named Bhat the last surviving active local militant, so his killing let Shah declare zero on 19 November.
But an estimated 40–50 foreign militants remain, so a threat persists. Separately, Shah did not define "India-born" or "locally recruited".
Shah blamed past poor coordination between state police and central agencies, and announced one uniform counter-terror strategy for every police station.

history.text: Kashmir's insurgency is widely linked to the 1987 state election, which many believed was rigged. The Muslim United Front won about 31% of the vote but only four seats. By 1989–90 armed insurgency had begun. Farooq Abdullah's government resigned on 19 January 1990, and an estimated 1,60,000–1,70,000 Kashmiri Hindus were displaced. That is roughly where Shah's "35 years" begins. In July 2016 the killing of militant Burhan Wani set off mass protests; over 100 civilians died and pellet guns blinded hundreds. By March 2017 government data counted about 41,000 deaths in the conflict. In February 2019 a Jaish-e-Mohammed suicide bomber killed 40 CRPF personnel at Pulwama. On 5 August 2019 Article 370 was abrogated, ending J&K's special status, and on 31 October 2019 J&K became two Union Territories. Counter-insurgency operations intensified, and militancy shifted to targeted killings of police, councillors and minorities. The Pahalgam attack on 22 April 2025 killed tourists and officials. Then, in February 2026, the Home Ministry set out PRAHAAR as India's first formal national counter-terror policy.

lesson.concept: How a militant headcount rises and falls
lesson.big_idea: A militant count is a snapshot: the starting number, minus those killed, arrested or surrendered, plus new recruits. Local and foreign are counted separately, so zero in one box can leave the other full.

steps.title: A count is a snapshot
steps.text: Security forces keep a running count of active militants: how many are armed and operating on a given day. It is like the balance in a bank account. In 2026, records cited by the media put the local count at one.

steps.title: What lowers and raises it
steps.text: The count falls when militants are killed, arrested or surrender. It rises when new people join, and, for foreign fighters, when more cross in. So: end count = start count − those removed + new joiners.

steps.title: Local and foreign are separate
steps.text: Shah did not define "local", so here we assume it means recruited from Jammu and Kashmir. Foreign means from outside; Shah has said these are mostly Pakistanis. In May 2025 records showed 17 local and nearly 60 foreign militants.

steps.title: Zero in one box
steps.text: A local count of zero leaves the foreign count untouched. It stays at zero only if recruitment stays at zero. And a different definition of "local" could change who lands in which box.

example.setup: Imagine a district starts the year with 10 local militants and 30 foreign ones. Over the year, security forces act, some young men join, and some fighters cross in.

lines.label: Local at start
lines.note: The stock on day one.

lines.label: Locals removed
lines.note: Each one lowers the count.

lines.label: Local at year end
lines.note: Start minus removed plus joiners.

lines.label: Foreign at year end
lines.note: Separate box, same rule.

lines.label: Total active
lines.note: Local is under a tenth of the total.

example.result: The local count fell from 10 to 3, but the total barely moved, from 40 to 33. And the local box reaches zero only if new recruitment also stops.

apply.text: Records showed 17 local militants in May 2025 and one in 2026. Police called Bhat the last one, so his killing on 18 November let Shah say the local box is empty. But the foreign box still holds an estimated 40–50, and it is not stated whether the Kishtwar suspects are local.

practice.q: Next year the same district starts with 3 local and 30 foreign militants. All 3 locals are killed and nobody joins. Four foreign are killed and two cross in. What are the counts?
practice.answer: Local: 3 − 3 + 0 = 0. Foreign: 30 − 4 + 2 = 28. Total: 0 + 28 = 28. The local box is empty, yet 28 militants are still active. Zero local is not zero overall.

stories.headline: Chase, Visa, Mastercard and EU hacks: where AI fits in
stories.question: Are AI tools behind the latest hacks at card companies and the EU Commission?
stories.dek: Only the EU Commission has called its attack AI-generated. The card firms' leaks came through outside vendors. AI's clearer effect is a flood of newly found software flaws that companies must rush to fix.

so_far.text: A software flaw that attackers can use is called a vulnerability. Since 1999, public flaws have been logged in a shared list called CVE. Big companies also hire outside vendors for jobs like marketing, and those vendors hold customer data. In 2026, companies began using AI models to hunt for flaws in their own code. Microsoft's monthly fixes rose from 415 in August to a record 1,413 in October. Meanwhile, a new extortion gang called n0n appeared in September 2026 and listed 108 victims in its first month.

what_happened.text: The extortion gang n0n claimed hacks of Chase, Visa and Mastercard and posted them on its leak site. On 19 November all three confirmed breaches at outside vendors. Chase said marketing data, possibly names and emails, was accessed. Mastercard said some emails from one benefit programme leaked. Visa said a provider in Asia Pacific was hit, but card numbers were not affected. None named the vendors or said when the breaches happened. Separately, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier called an attack detected on 22 October "an AI-generated cybercampaign". The Commission took several applications offline as a precaution.

steps.text: Big firms give customer data to outside vendors for jobs like marketing, so a vendor breach exposes the firm's customers.
Extortion gangs like n0n steal that data and post victims on leak sites to pressure them.
Separately, AI models now find software flaws far faster, so companies must release many more fixes.
Rushed fixes can break systems; the Financial Times reported recent US outages were blamed on this rush.
Only the Commission says attackers used AI, and it has not said how or who was behind it.

history.text:
The story starts in 1999, when MITRE launched the CVE list, a public catalogue of software flaws. It held 321 records that year. In 2005 NIST, a US standards agency, built the National Vulnerability Database on top of it. That gave defenders one shared record of every known flaw. Totals kept rising: from 6,447 in 2016 to 14,714 in 2017, a 128% jump. By October 2024 the list had passed 240,000 records.

Attackers learned that a supplier is often the easiest door. In May 2023 the Russia-linked Cl0p group exploited a flaw in the MOVEit file-transfer tool. It hit over 2,700 organisations and exposed data on about 93–96 million people. In 2024 the group UNC5537 got into at least 165 Snowflake customer accounts using stolen login details, not a software flaw. Both cases showed the risk sitting with outside providers.

The European Commission was hacked twice earlier in 2026. Staff names and some phone numbers were taken from its mobile-device system, reported in January and February. On 24 March its Amazon Web Services account was breached.

Then AI sped up bug-hunting. Mozilla said Anthropic's Mythos model helped it find and fix over 270 Firefox flaws. Microsoft, using AI to scan its code, went from 415 fixes in August to a record 1,413 in October. In September the gang n0n appeared.

lesson.concept: Why finding bugs faster starts a patching race
lesson.big_idea: A software flaw is dangerous until it is fixed. When AI finds flaws faster than teams can safely fix them, unfixed flaws pile up, and rushing the fixes can break things.

steps.title: A flaw is an open window
steps.text: A vulnerability is a mistake in code that lets someone do what they shouldn't. Publicly known ones get an ID on the CVE list, which MITRE launched in 1999.

steps.title: Fixing takes time
steps.text: Each fix, called a patch, must be written, tested and installed. Testing matters: a patch that clashes with older systems can crash a service people depend on.

steps.title: AI speeds up finding
steps.text: AI models can read huge amounts of code and flag flaws quickly. Using them, Microsoft fixed 1,413 flaws in October 2026, more than its roughly 1,273 for all of 2025.

steps.title: The gap becomes a backlog
steps.text: If flaws are found faster than they are fixed, the unfixed pile, or backlog, grows every month. Each flaw in that pile is a window an attacker might also find.

steps.title: Rushing has its own cost
steps.text: Teams under pressure may cut testing to clear the backlog. The Financial Times reported that recent US tech outages were blamed on this rush to fix AI-found bugs.

example.setup: Imagine a small software team that can safely test and release 20 fixes a month. Before AI it found 10 flaws a month. Assume AI tools now help it find 50.

lines.label: Before AI
lines.note: Capacity of 20 is more than enough; no backlog.

lines.label: With AI, each month
lines.note: Finding now outpaces safe fixing.

lines.label: After three months
lines.note: The backlog grows every month.

lines.label: The rush option
lines.note: Backlog stops growing, but untested fixes may crash systems.

example.result: Finding more flaws helps only if fixing keeps pace. Otherwise you get a growing pile of known, open flaws, or rushed fixes that break the very systems you are protecting.

apply.text: Microsoft's fixes jumped from 415 in August to 1,413 in October as it used AI to hunt bugs. Dave DeWalt says many of these flaws already existed and the patch rush is disrupting systems; Anusha Iyer blames rushed mixing of old and new systems. Chase blamed its outage that week on a software bug, and said it was unrelated to the breach.

practice.q: Same team, but it hires help and can now safely fix 40 flaws a month while AI finds 50. How big is the backlog after six months?
practice.answer: Each month: 50 found − 40 fixed = 10 left over. Over six months: 10 × 6 = 60 unfixed flaws. That is far smaller than the 180 it would have had at 20 fixes a month, but it is still growing.

Har fix, jise patch kehte hain, likhna, test karna aur install karna padta hai. Testing chhodi, toh patch service crash kar sakta hai.
scenes.speak: अब वो idea जिससे सब समझ आता है: patching race. Flaw code की एक ग़लती है जिससे कोई अंदर घुस सकता है। जब तक ठीक न हो, ख़तरा बना रहता है। हर fix, जिसे patch कहते हैं, लिखना, test करना और install करना पड़ता है। Testing छोड़ी, तो patch service crash कर सकता है।

scenes.say: Ab isme AI jodiye. Yeh bahut saara code padhta hai aur flaws jaldi pakadta hai. Agar flaws theek hone se tez mil rahe hain, toh bina fix wala dher har mahine badhta hai. Har ek khuli khidki hai. Dabaav mein teams fixes jaldbaazi mein nikaal sakti hain.
scenes.speak: अब इसमें AI जोड़िए। यह बहुत सारा code पढ़ता है और flaws जल्दी पकड़ता है। अगर flaws ठीक होने से तेज़ मिल रहे हैं, तो बिना fix वाला ढेर हर महीने बढ़ता है। हर एक खुली खिड़की है। दबाव में teams fixes जल्दबाज़ी में निकाल सकती हैं।

scenes.say: Maan lijiye ek team mahine mein 20 flaws safely theek kar sakti hai. AI se pehle woh 10 dhoondhti thi, toh kuch jama nahi hua. Ab maan lo AI 50 dhoondhta hai. 50 minus 20, yaani har mahine 30 bina fix. 3 mahine baad, 90 khule flaws. Ya phir team saare 50 bina test nikaal de.
scenes.speak: मान लीजिए एक team महीने में 20 flaws safely ठीक कर सकती है। AI से पहले वो 10 ढूँढती थी, तो कुछ जमा नहीं हुआ। अब मान लो AI 50 ढूँढता है। 50 minus 20, यानी हर महीने 30 बिना fix. 3 महीने बाद, 90 खुले flaws. या फिर team सारे 50 बिना test निकाल दे।

scenes.say: Raaye alag hain. Dave DeWalt kehte hain AI purane flaws ko aisi speed se saamne la raha hai jo pehle kabhi nahi dekhi, aur patch ki jaldbaazi systems bigaad rahi hai. Corsha ki Anusha Iyer iske bajaye purane aur naye systems ki jaldbaazi wali mixing ko dosh deti hain. Thomas Regnier Commission attack ko AI-generated kehte hain, par staff-wide breach nahi dekhte.
scenes.speak: राय अलग हैं। Dave DeWalt कहते हैं AI पुराने flaws को ऐसी speed से सामने ला रहा है जो पहले कभी नहीं देखी, और patch की जल्दबाज़ी systems बिगाड़ रही है। Corsha की Anusha Iyer इसके बजाय पुराने और नए systems की जल्दबाज़ी वाली mixing को दोष देती हैं। Thomas Regnier Commission attack को AI-generated कहते हैं, पर staff-wide breach नहीं देखते।

views.view: AI surfaces old flaws at record speed; patch rush disrupts systems
Not AI directly; rushed mixing of old and new systems
AI-generated campaign; no evidence of staff-wide breach

scenes.say: Ek aam myth: hackers card companies ke payment systems mein ghus gaye. Companies aisa nahi kehti. Visa kehta hai card numbers aur uske apne systems shaamil nahi the. Mastercard kehta hai uske payment network par asar nahi hua. Chase kehta hai uski services ruki nahi.
scenes.show: All three blame an outside vendor
scenes.speak: एक आम myth: hackers card companies के payment systems में घुस गए। Companies ऐसा नहीं कहतीं। Visa कहता है card numbers और उसके अपने systems शामिल नहीं थे। Mastercard कहता है उसके payment network पर असर नहीं हुआ। Chase कहता है उसकी services रुकी नहीं।

scenes.say: India mein aapke liye iska kya matlab hai? Koi source nahi kehta ki Indian cardholders par asar hua, haalanki Visa ka provider Asia Pacific mein tha. Card users ke liye koi official salaah nahi mili. Ek general ehtiyaat ke taur par, card breach ka koi bhi message apne bank ke official app ya helpline se check kijiye.
scenes.show: No sign Indian cardholders were hit
scenes.speak: India में आपके लिए इसका क्या मतलब है? कोई source नहीं कहता कि Indian cardholders पर असर हुआ, हालाँकि Visa का provider Asia Pacific में था। Card users के लिए कोई official सलाह नहीं मिली। एक general एहतियात के तौर पर, card breach का कोई भी message अपने bank के official app या helpline से check कीजिए।

scenes.say: Aur hamara sabak? AI use karte hue Microsoft ke fixes August se October tak teen guna se zyada ho gaye. Yahi hai patching race. Chase aur Visa kehte hain breaches ka us hafte ke service outages se koi lena-dena nahi; Chase ne apne outage ka dosh on-premise hardware ke ek software bug par diya.
scenes.show: Outages unrelated to breaches, firms say
scenes.speak: और हमारा सबक? AI use करते हुए Microsoft के fixes August से October तक तीन गुना से ज़्यादा हो गए। यही है patching race. Chase और Visa कहते हैं breaches का उस हफ़्ते के service outages से कोई लेना-देना नहीं; Chase ने अपने outage का दोष on-premise hardware के एक software bug पर दिया।

scenes.say: Aage kya? Koi date tay nahi hai. Dekhiye ki companies apne vendors ke naam batati hain ya nahi, Chase customers se sampark karta hai ya nahi, aur Commission batata hai ya nahi ki hamla kisne kiya aur kaunsa AI tool use hua. Yeh bhi pata nahi ki Commission ka koi personal data gaya ya nahi.
scenes.show: Watch: vendors named, AI tool revealed
scenes.speak: आगे क्या? कोई date तय नहीं है। देखिए कि companies अपने vendors के नाम बताती हैं या नहीं, Chase customers से संपर्क करता है या नहीं, और Commission बताता है या नहीं कि हमला किसने किया और कौनसा AI tool use हुआ। यह भी पता नहीं कि Commission का कोई personal data गया या नहीं।

scenes.say: Teen baatein yaad rakhiye. AI flaws tezi se dhoondhta hai; agar fixing saath na de paaye, toh khule flaws jama hote hain ya jaldbaazi ke fixes cheezein todte hain. Card leaks outside vendors ke raaste aaye. Aur nazar rakhiye vendor ke naamon par, aur Commission ke khilaaf AI kaise use hua, us par.
scenes.show: Faster finding needs faster, safe fixing
scenes.speak: तीन बातें याद रखिए। AI flaws तेज़ी से ढूँढता है; अगर fixing साथ न दे पाए, तो खुले flaws जमा होते हैं या जल्दबाज़ी के fixes चीज़ें तोड़ते हैं। Card leaks outside vendors के रास्ते आए। और नज़र रखिए vendor के नामों पर, और Commission के ख़िलाफ़ AI कैसे use हुआ, उस पर।
